title: Mirra Andreeva has taken the WTA Finals by storm. Now she must embrace the pressure
content:
INDIAN WELLS, Calif. — Mirra Andreeva can’t seem to help it. Something about the California desert brings out the diva in her.

The 19-year-old from Russia has had some of the highest and lowest moments of her career at Indian Wells, Calif. The spectrum of experiences now includes Saturday’s 6-3, 6-4 win over Jessica Pegula, which took her to the championship match at the WTA Finals.

She will face Elina Svitolina in the final Sunday, in a matchup that emphasizes the uniqueness of this tournament. Andreeva entered as a debutant and started her run in the middle of a hot mic hot mess, after Pegula was caught calling her a “diva” in what she thought was a private conversation with one of her coaches.

From there, Andreeva won her three round-robin matches at a canter, including 6-4, 6-0 demolitions of Svitolina and Aryna Sabalenka. In the process, the new face at the event became an overwhelming favorite. Then, Andreeva faced Pegula, in a match that still had a little extra, even though it came days after they had put any ill-feeling to bed. She won that match handily too, to reach the final without dropping a set.

Svitolina, meantime, responded to that opening loss by going a set down to Karolína Muchová in her second match, with Muchová holding a break point for a 6-2, 3-1 lead. Svitolina saved it, and started a remarkable transformation. She came back to win, before defeating Sabalenka for the first time in six years to reach the semifinals, where she dismissed Wimbledon champion Linda Nosková.

Now she and Andreeva meet again, on a much bigger stage. Svitolina, 32, is back in the championship match on her first appearance in seven years, while Andreeva is the youngest finalist since Maria Sharapova in 2004. Since the WTA Finals began in 1972, she is the second-youngest player to win her first four matches, after Chris Evert. Her methodical dismantling of Pegula Saturday means she will end the year as world No. 2.

Andreeva did a little dance at that in her post-match news conference, before taking a moment to compose a more thorough response.

“It’s nice to be No. 2 in the world, but it’s not far from being No. 3 in the world,” Andreeva said. “I was No. 3 in the world last week, so I don’t know if a lot changes with how I feel inside. But of course, it’s a nice milestone.”

It feels fitting that she should achieve that milestone at Indian Wells, where it is easy to chart the arc of Andreeva’s growth into a champion.

In March 2025, she won the first WTA 1000 title of her career at the BNP Paribas Open, defeating Sabalenka in the final. A year later, she had the biggest public meltdown of her career.

Now, Andreeva prepares to play for the WTA Finals trophy at the end of a landmark season, during which she won her first Grand Slam and dealt with the mental, emotional and physical fallout that often discombobulates first-time major champions. She isn’t a new Andreeva — she still carries around plushies, skips up to interviews after wins and shields neither her joy nor her sorrow.

But she does feel a bit more adept at riding the roller coaster of professional tennis. The emotional pendulum swings that come with her job are perfectly normal. It’s how she deals with them that matters.

“Sometimes you’re gonna have great results. Sometimes you’re just gonna lose in first and second round, and that’s also okay a few weeks. So, I don’t know. The most important is how you kind of approach the next tournaments that you have and learn from the losses and try to move forward,” Andreeva said.

In March, Andreeva was fraying under the pressure of defending her Indian Wells title. She lost her second-round match to Kateřina Siniaková and erupted on her way out of the stadium, waving a hand at the crowd as she said, “f––– you all, f––– you all.”

Andreeva acknowledged her misstep when she apologized for her behavior, but she also gave tennis fans one of the more indelible moments of the year: A video clip of a stunned — and somewhat delighted — spectator watching Andreeva’s exit with her mouth agape, before clutching her necklace in mild horror.

Andreeva’s emotional outbursts continued despite strong play during the clay-court season. She berated herself during a fourth-round match against Hungary’s Anna Bondár at the Madrid Open, saying to her coach, Conchita Martínez, “I’m not a champion, I’m not a champion. I will lose. I will lose. I choke.”

She won, and then crowned her time on the red dirt with the French Open title, the first major of her career. But it took her time to take full measure of just what she had achieved with that milestone. Her second-round loss at Wimbledon, with hardly any time to adjust to a surface change or process achieving a dream, brought tears in a post-match news conference.

Back at Indian Wells eight months after her outburst at the BNP Paribas Open, Andreeva began her first WTA Finals under a spotlight after Pegula’s comments went viral. The WTA apologized for not informing players that practice courts were mic’d up, while Pegula apologized to Andreeva in person as soon as she could. It was quickly water under the bridge between the two, who joked about the incident several times after.

Pegula also hadn’t said anything that struck tennis fans as particularly false. Andreeva, by her own admission, can be a diva. In a mixed-zone interview this week, she said that losses used to mean a two or three-day pity party where she wouldn’t talk to anyone, practice or leave her room much.

It takes less time for her to move on now, maybe a day before she gets back to her job. She watched every video and consumed all the social media posts about the incident in March. This week, she has taken everything in her stride, and now the tournament’s unique format means she must do something she did less than a week ago, under a much greater spotlight. For Svitolina, there is the opportunity for redemption, and to crown one of the best seasons of her career.

“I’m happy with how I dealt with the pressure,” Andreeva said after beating Pegula. “I’m happy with how composed I was able to be throughout the match.”
